title: Fairlearn: Assessing and Improving Fairness of AI Systems
harvard_reference: Weerts, H., Dudík, M., Edgar, R., Jalali, A., Lutz, R. and Madaio, M. (2023) 'Fairlearn: assessing and improving fairness of AI systems', Journal of Machine Learning Research, 24(257), pp. 1-8. Available at: https://jmlr.org/papers/v24/23-0389.html (Accessed: 27 September 2026).
abstract_summary: An eight-page JMLR 'Machine Learning Open Source Software' paper by the current maintainers of Fairlearn (Eindhoven University of Technology and Microsoft). Fairlearn is an MIT-licensed open-source project (started at Microsoft in 2018, under independent governance since 2021) consisting of the Python library fairlearn plus learning resources. The abstract states that the library supports evaluation of a model's output across affected populations and includes several algorithms for mitigating fairness issues, and that the project treats fairness as a sociotechnical challenge. Section 2 (Fairness Assessment) describes disaggregated evaluation via the MetricFrame class in fairlearn.metrics (metric functions plus y_true, y_pred and sensitive_features; results returned as pandas Series/DataFrame; group comparison by differences or ratios), scalar fairness metrics such as demographic_parity_difference and equalized_odds_difference (derived from a MetricFrame), make_derived_metric, and plot_model_comparison. Section 3 covers mitigation algorithms: preprocessing (CorrelationRemover), reductions-based in-processing (ExponentiatedGradient, GridSearch, following Agarwal et al. 2018), adversarial mitigation, and postprocessing (ThresholdOptimizer, following Hardt et al. 2016), all with scikit-learn-compatible APIs. Section 4 describes the learning resources (user guide, example notebooks) that encourage practitioners to consider a system's broader societal context rather than treating fairness metrics as a purely technical fix.

claims_supported.claim: Fairlearn provides MetricFrame for disaggregated metrics by sensitive feature and standard group-fairness metrics such as demographic parity and equalised odds differences.
claims_supported.where: Section 2, 'Fairness Assessment', p. 2 of the JMLR PDF. Paragraph 'MetricFrame class': 'The primary tool for disaggregated evaluation in the fairlearn library is the MetricFrame class in the fairlearn.metrics module ... MetricFrame is initialized by providing one or more metric functions together with input arrays y_true, y_pred, and sensitive_features ... the sensitive_features array is used to split the data into slices for disaggregated evaluation. Once a MetricFrame is constructed, the disaggregated metrics can be accessed as a pandas Series ... or a pandas DataFrame ... MetricFrame also enables a comparison of metric values across groups, for example, in terms of differences or ratios.' Paragraph 'Fairness Metrics': 'functions demographic_parity_difference and equalized_odds_difference quantify how much the predictions of a given classifier depart from the fairness criteria known as demographic parity and equalized odds (see, e.g., Hardt et al., 2016). These two metrics are derived from a MetricFrame with a specific choice of input arguments.' Every element of the claim (MetricFrame, disaggregation by sensitive feature, demographic parity difference, equalized odds difference) is stated explicitly in the paper's own text, not merely in the documentation.

verification_notes: Crossref query.bibliographic did NOT return this paper (only unrelated Packt book chapters and an IEEE paper), which is expected because JMLR does not register Crossref DOIs for its articles; the doi field is therefore left empty rather than invented. The article was verified directly on the publisher's site: the JMLR landing page https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v24/23-0389.html gives the title, the six authors in order (Hilde Weerts, Miroslav Dudík, Richard Edgar, Adrin Jalali, Roman Lutz, Michael Madaio), the citation '24(257):1-8, 2023' and the abstract; the JMLR BibTeX file (https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v24/23-0389.bib) confirms journal, year 2023, volume 24, number 257, pages 1--8. The official PDF (https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume24/23-0389/23-0389.pdf, 8 pages) was downloaded and its text extracted; the header reads 'Journal of Machine Learning Research 24 (2023) 1-8 Submitted 3/23; Published 7/23', editor Alexandre Gramfort, affiliations Eindhoven University of Technology (Weerts) and Microsoft (Dudík, Edgar, Lutz, Madaio; Madaio's listed e-mail is at google.com). The claim was checked against the extracted full text of Section 2. OpenAlex (W4361806824) indexes the work as JMLR vol. 24, issue 257, 2023, with the same six authors, but the only DOI it attaches is the arXiv/DataCite DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2303.16626, which belongs to the preprint (arXiv:2303.16626, submitted 29 March 2023, verified on arxiv.org) rather than to the JMLR version; hence the Harvard reference uses the JMLR URL with an access date, per Cite Them Right for online articles without a DOI. The earlier work mentioned in the lead is confirmed by the paper's own reference list and footnote 3: Bird, S., Dudík, M., Edgar, R., Horn, B., Lutz, R., Milan, V., Sameki, M., Wallach, H. and Walker, K. (2020) Fairlearn: a toolkit for assessing and improving fairness in AI, Technical Report MSR-TR-2020-32, Microsoft, May 2020, https://aka.ms/fairlearn-whitepaper (also indexed by OpenAlex as W3030081171). The Semantic Scholar API returned HTTP 429 and was not used. The lead's metadata was accurate apart from omitting the page range (pp. 1-8).
caveats: This is a short software paper, not an empirical study on churn or telecom data; cite it for what the Fairlearn library provides (MetricFrame, fairness metrics, mitigation algorithms), not for any finding about fairness in churn models. The paper describes the API as of 2023 (fairlearn ~0.8); function names such as demographic_parity_difference and equalized_odds_difference match the current library, but any specific version-dependent behaviour should be cited to the Fairlearn documentation. The paper's own framing (Section 4) cautions against treating fairness metrics as a purely technical fix, which the report should reflect when interpreting parity gaps on the Telco dataset (e.g. by SeniorCitizen or gender). If the report also cites the 2020 Microsoft technical report (Bird et al., 2020), that is a separate grey-literature reference (MSR-TR-2020-32) and should be listed separately.
